title: What do you want? (Luke 18:31–43)
hookLine: a blind beggar at Jericho shouts, and Jesus stops the whole procession

cards: Just before Jericho, Jesus takes the twelve aside and tells them plainly what's coming in Jerusalem: he'll be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, killed, and on the third day rise again.
And Luke adds an almost sad sentence: "And they understood none of these things: and this saying was hid from them." They have eyes. They've seen everything.
And they can't see. Then, outside Jericho, they meet a man who has no eyesight at all.

teach.h: SON OF DAVID: HE SEES WHO HE IS.
teach.b: Luke doesn't name him; Mark calls him Bartimaeus. He's begging by the roadside, hears a crowd, and asks what's happening. Jesus of Nazareth is passing.
And he shouts, in the King James Bible: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." Son of David is a title for the promised king. The man who can't see is the one who sees who Jesus is.
The people at the front tell him to be quiet.

teach.h: HE CRIED SO MUCH THE MORE.
teach.b: "But he cried so much the more."
Then: "And Jesus stood, and commanded him to be brought unto him." A whole crowd on the road to Jerusalem, and it stops for one beggar.
Then a question that sounds too obvious: "What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?" Jesus asks anyway, letting the man say it himself, as a person with a voice and not just a problem.

teach.h: LORD, THAT I MAY RECEIVE MY SIGHT.
teach.b: "Lord, that I may receive my sight." The Greek verb can mean see again, and it can mean look up. "And immediately he received his sight, and followed him, glorifying God."
Up the road to Jerusalem, toward everything the disciples couldn't understand.
Look at the week: a beggar with a name, faith the size of a seed, one who turned back to give thanks, a kingdom in your midst, babies carried forward, a ruler who couldn't let go.
And now a blind man who could see, a shout that stopped a crowd, and a question: what do you want?

how: Some Christians hear the blind man's cry, have mercy on me, in the Jesus Prayer that Orthodox Christians and others repeat, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me; the story is also read when praying for healing and for spiritual sight.

games.q: you're blind, begging by the road to Jericho. you've shouted for Jesus, and the crowd tells you to shut up. what do you do?
o: go quiet. they're right, he's busy.
try to follow the noise on your own.
games.why: "he cried so much the more," and Jesus stood, and commanded him to be brought, and asked: what wilt thou?

practice: Think of the voices around you asking for help, some loud, some quiet: a friend who keeps mentioning a hard time, a family member who calls too often.
Imagine your day halting the way the crowd did, and asking one of them: what do you want me to do for you? Listen for their answer, not yours, and if you pray, ask for eyes to see who's calling.

wordCard.voice: Bartimaeus, the blind beggar outside Jericho, unnamed in Luke and named by Mark, whose shout stopped a whole crowd.

orig.note: Greek: that I may see again. the verb can also mean to look up.

carryVoice: Your line: Jesus stood still. One voice was enough to stop him. Day five hundred sixty-seven, and another week on the path.
